entries.q: Who is the opening prayer addressed to, and what does he do?
entries.a: Śiva — giver of kaivalya (final solitary freedom), praised as a sun that burnt away the darkness on every road of becoming.

entries.q: What does pure awareness cut?
entries.a: Śuddhasaṃvid (pure awareness) is the only knife that cuts the heart's knot of 'mine' and 'I'. It swallowed both throbbing and its stillness.

entries.q: How can something that can't be named ever be known?
entries.a: It cannot be named. Anyone who reaches it at all does so by svasaṃvedana (honestly feeling oneself) — no other method.

entries.q: What is the actual practice for reaching the goal?
entries.a: Stay awake in your own svabodha (self-awakening). From such waking the sage stands whole and undivided — that is the whole way.

entries.q: What happens when you hold your own thoughts still?
entries.a: When your own thought is gripped still, śakti (the power) rests in the śaktimat (holder of power). Their oneness is what yogis are after.

entries.q: What has to happen for a person to be called free?
entries.a: Know your svarūpa (own form), drop the tattvakañcuka (veil of principles), and scatter the cause of striving. Then you are called free.

entries.q: Is liberation hard to win?
entries.a: Not for yogis grounded in themselves whose single mind sweeps aside the traces of grasping and the grasped. For them mokṣalakṣmī (fortune's release) is not hard to gain.

entries.q: What stops you from taking a body again?
entries.a: Nairvāsanya (wanting nothing), self-waking, dropping hope and pride, and cutting the road of real-and-unreal. From those, no taking of a body again.

entries.q: Who is praised before the argument even starts?
entries.a: The one God — Maheśvara (the great Lord). A single maker, praised in one line.

entries.q: Why can't bare matter produce an ordered world?
entries.a: Bodies and worlds show a distinct array in arthakriyā (function-yoking). This arrangement, the verse says, never arises from mere matter.

entries.q: What conclusion does the verse draw from all this variety?
entries.a: Conscious makers are proved, so the Lord's act is proved. To anyone who knows such variety, anīśitā (lordlessness) is impossible.

entries.q: What is the objection being raised against the rival school?
entries.a: The rival's pradhāna (nature-principle) — three-natured, a torrent of change from the first — leaves the world godless. That is the Sāṅkhya view, called out here.

entries.q: What everyday example does the verse use to prove a maker?
entries.a: A pot needs a potter. Without the potter, the verse says, not even a pot could come about.

entries.q: Why do some people still not accept the proof?
entries.a: A thousand blazing reasons prove it, yet it does not succeed for deluded minds. Maheśvara sits on your palm and still runs from the fate-struck — like a true jewel.

entries.q: Where does the work say the Lord actually is?
entries.a: Inside every breather — the maker and the knower of each. Pratyabhijñā (recognition) of the beyond is still to be effected; the proved Lord stands even in duality, like fire shining at midnight.

entries.q: Is there really a difference between living and non-living things?
entries.a: The verse says no. Just as there is no difference between the real and the unreal in their own nature, so there is none between jaḍa (utterly inert) and the non-inert.

entries.q: If everything is really undifferentiated, why do some things work and others don't?
entries.a: The existent performs arthakriyā (a real function) and the nonexistent does not. Yet in its own self the thing remains without distinction.

entries.q: What does everything finally rest on?
entries.a: Function is not what is described in a thing whose existence is already established; the two stand exactly on par. So their grounding rests on saṃvid (consciousness itself).

entries.q: What would go wrong if awareness never grasped anything?
entries.a: If consciousness were aparāmarśa (never grasping), it would itself be exactly equal to inert non-being — the same as before. Awareness has to grasp.

entries.q: How does awareness establish other things and itself?
entries.a: By saying 'this' it grounds the showing of another thing; by saying 'I' it grounds itself. One awareness, two acts.

entries.q: Is the self one thing or two?
entries.a: One self, twofold — measured and unmeasured. Held by breath and the rest it is an atom; as paramātman (supreme self) it is unbroken.

entries.q: What is Māyā, in this text's own words?
entries.a: Māyā is his śakti (his own power) alone — nothing else is proved. The world-maker's lordship is made of akhyāti (simply non-showing).

entries.q: What does recognition actually claim about the world?
entries.a: Even within bheda (real difference) the shining holds good. So pratyabhijñā (recognition) says: this world is made of that one nondual.

entries.q: Who is praised, and what kind of relation is his?
entries.a: Śiva, praised by his own will. His saṃbandha (means of relation) to things is difference-and-non-difference at once, and by it all things are proved — his work is world-traffic.

entries.q: Why isn't mere continuity enough to count as a relation?
entries.a: Continuity misses relation entirely — if it counted, it would hold between two iron bars. So relation means fusion of the many's forms; that alone is aikātmya (one-selfhood).

entries.q: What exactly is an error, according to this verse?
entries.a: Not something that merely resembles a shining. It is following after a shining — ābhāsa (a shining astray) is exactly what error is.

entries.q: How do many separate things come to be seen as one?
entries.a: By resting in the reflection of that one, through the force of one-word superimposition. The many reach unity, the way 'pot' and 'cloth' are said together.

entries.q: How can two things be joined without either losing itself?
entries.a: The ṣaṣṭhī (genitive case) relation settles in the qualifier: reaching the qualified-oneness, it does not abandon its own form.

entries.q: What actually holds an ordinary person's world together?
entries.a: Even those called erring are, moment by moment, grounded in svasaṃvitti (endless self-awareness) — reflection that never runs out.

entries.q: What has this whole teaching been for?
entries.a: Self-awareness-proved: a saṃbandha (means of relation) unrefuted and useful — the full apparatus for pratyabhijñā (recognition).

entries.q: Who or what is the cause of the universe here?
entries.a: Citi (free consciousness) is the universe's cause, so called. The knower is freedom-formed, and she bestows powers too.

entries.q: Where does mind come from?
entries.a: From citi-saṅkoca (consciousness tightening). Mind is a knower too — even the great Lord — and the world-form sits there like a banyan seed.

entries.q: Is mind the same thing as pure knowing?
entries.a: Yes. Caitanya (pure knowing) is the self's form — stainless, utterly stainless. That same knowing, bound by niyama (rule), is called mind.

entries.q: Who is the great Lord described in this verse?
entries.a: One, everywhere, pure, sambodhātma (awareness-selfed) — Maheśvara. From mis-knowing that I-ness, mukti (freedom) sits in the palm.

entries.q: Are the stages of a real spiritual path fixed?
entries.a: They are kṛtrima (stages made up): as an actor assumes roles by his own will, so the bliss-will-spread self assumes vast views-and-powers.

entries.q: What makes the self a wanderer instead of a power-lord?
entries.a: Vikāsa (expansion) sings him as śaktīśa (power-Lord). Saṅkoca (contraction) makes him contracted — called saṃsārī (the wandering one), like the great god doing the five acts, deluded by power.

entries.q: What does constant practice of true reflection produce?
entries.a: Whoever always practices by sadvimarśa (true reflection) is freed from all bonds and becomes full of nityānanda (eternal bliss).

entries.q: What is this teaching called, and what does it do?
entries.a: Jñānāmṛta (nectar of knowledge), unsurpassed. Whoever drinks it is quenched — his fever of saṃsāra-poison subsides.

entries.q: Is God mere light, or does He actually know?
entries.a: Prakāśa (light) is vimarśa-svabhāva (awareness-natured). Creating, awareness wears the world's shape; sustaining, it shines the world forth; withdrawing, it takes all back — everywhere a full and complete I.

entries.q: Why does one awareness get so many names in scripture?
entries.a: Each name is earned by its work: cit (consciousness) as the Self's chief form, svātantrya (freedom) binding and loosing the this, kartṛtva (doership) raising the world, hṛdaya (heart) where the world rests.

entries.q: How can the world be 'made' by God if it isn't separate from Him?
entries.a: Made means shining-by-Him. The world is nothing apart from its maker — without His light it could not even be noticed. Māyā's own freedom puts difference on display while nothing differs.

entries.q: Does the Lord need to be proved?
entries.a: No. Proofs cannot grip Him, proved before all proof. Svaprakāśatva (self-shining) is proved for everyone by feeling oneself — the questioner's own shape is the proof.

entries.q: What are the thirty-six levels of reality?
entries.a: The whole display from Śiva down to the five gross elements — thirty-six tattva (levels of reality): Śiva, power, eternal Śiva, the Lord, pure knowledge, illusion, art, knowing, passion, time, necessity, person, nature, intellect, ego, mind, the senses, the elements.

entries.q: How does the Lord become a bound, wandering person?
entries.a: By pārameśvarī śakti (the Lady's power of illusion) — only another name for freedom — He veils His own form and puts on the tight mask of knowerhood, then takes his deeds for chains.

entries.q: What keeps an all-knowing being from knowing everything?
entries.a: Five coverings: kañcuka (the sheath) of art, knowing, passion, time and necessity — each makes him do or know only a little. They veil His own form.

entries.q: Where is the whole world stored?
entries.a: Inside hṛdaya-bīja (the heart-seed), as the whole banyan stands in its seed. Whoever truly knows that heart-seed is initiated in truth, and is free while living.
